title: New Scientist Story Ideas — September 2026

studies.title: Postpartum depression is strongly heritable, Danish twin study finds
studies.ns_score_reason: first twin-design heritability estimate for postpartum depression in a whole-population register, though it rests on a small number of concordant pairs.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (2 news hits)
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers linked the Danish Twin Register to national health registers, identifying 10,418 female twins (5209 pairs) born 1949–2000 who had given birth. Postpartum depression was defined by hospital diagnosis or filled antidepressant prescription in the first year after delivery. Identical twins were roughly twice as concordant as fraternal twins (0.22 versus 0.11), giving a heritability estimate of 0.60, with the remaining 40 percent attributed to non-shared environment.
studies.why_it_matters: Postpartum depression has long been framed either as a hormonal accident or as a failure of coping; a genetic contribution on a par with that of major depression reframes it as a condition women are predisposed to, and the authors explicitly pitch this as an anti-stigma finding.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the number — well over half of the variation in who gets postpartum depression tracks with genes, from the country with the world's best birth and prescription registers. Open on a woman whose sister or mother had it. Call Trine Munk-Olsen or Mette Bliddal (University of Southern Denmark), who have built much of the population-scale perinatal psychiatry evidence base, and ask what a heritability figure can and cannot tell an individual mother.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health or parenting outlet on how far perinatal mental health screening has moved from symptom checklists toward family history and, eventually, polygenic risk — and the ethical unease of telling a pregnant woman she is "at risk" when no preventive treatment is guaranteed.
studies.caveats: Observational and register-based (no interviews); only 15 concordant pairs in total, so confidence intervals are wide; antidepressant prescriptions are an imperfect proxy for depression; Danish-only population may not generalize; author funding from the Novo Nordisk and Lundbeck Foundations, with Lundbeck lecture fees declared.

studies.title: Insomnia travels with PTSD and depression but does not seem to cause them
studies.ns_score_reason: a 10-year, six-wave military cohort directly contradicts the widely repeated claim that poor sleep drives later mental illness; limited by self-report subscales.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (2 news hits)
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: The Dutch PRISMO cohort followed 846 deployed military personnel from before deployment to 1 month, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years and 10 years afterwards, measuring insomnia, depression and PTSD symptoms. Using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model, which separates within-person change from stable individual differences, insomnia symptoms did not predict later PTSD or depression. Instead, all three rose and fell together at every time point, while PTSD and depression showed small reciprocal effects on each other.
studies.why_it_matters: "Fix the sleep to prevent the PTSD" has become a standard assumption in military and civilian mental health; this suggests insomnia is a co-traveler reflecting shared vulnerability rather than an upstream cause — which matters for how prevention trials are designed and sold.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is a negative: ten years of data on soldiers before and after deployment find that bad sleep does not come first. Open on the standard advice given to returning personnel. Call Elbert Geuze or Eric Vermetten (PRISMO cohort), and ask how this squares with insomnia-treatment trials that do improve PTSD symptoms — the within-person modeling is the crux of the argument.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-led feature for a science or psychology outlet on how cross-lagged panel models have been quietly demolishing a generation of "X predicts Y" findings once between-person differences are stripped out — sleep, screen time, exercise and mood all in the firing line.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation in either direction); insomnia and depression measured only as SCL-90 subscales, not clinical insomnia diagnoses; military sample is mostly young and male and may not generalize; long gap between the 2-year and 10-year waves.

studies.title: Twelve minutes of vigorous exercise a week matches 150 minutes of moderate activity
studies.journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
studies.ns_score_reason: the largest pooled device-measured activity dataset yet, with a strikingly small vigorous-activity threshold; still observational, and short follow-up for mortality.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled wrist accelerometer data from 147,414 adults aged 40–74 in the German National Cohort and UK Biobank and followed them for a mean 7.9 years, during which 5545 died. Compared with no activity, 150 minutes a week of moderate activity was associated with a 30 percent lower mortality risk — and so was about 510 minutes of light activity or roughly 12 minutes of vigorous activity. Statistically swapping just 15–60 minutes a week of light or moderate activity for vigorous activity was associated with 18–30 percent lower risk.
studies.why_it_matters: Guidelines are written in units of moderate activity; these numbers suggest intensity buys disproportionate returns at very low volumes, and that "not enough time" is a weaker excuse than assumed.
studies.pitch_angle: Twelve minutes. That is the headline, and it comes from accelerometers rather than the notoriously flattering activity questionnaires. Open on someone who walks a lot but never gets out of breath. Call Michael Stein or Michael Leitzmann (University of Regensburg / Helmholtz Munich) and press them on reverse causation — people who can sprint are people who are already well.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist sport-science or policy outlet: are public health guidelines still using the wrong currency? A piece on the push to rewrite activity recommendations around intensity and "exercise snacks," and why moderate-intensity minutes became the unit in the first place.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation); baseline activity measured once, over about a week; reverse causality from undiagnosed illness is a real risk despite adjustment; UK Biobank and NAKO participants are healthier and more affluent than the general population; one co-author declares Bayer and Siemens Healthineers funding.

studies.title: "Food noise" is quieter in people six months into GLP-1 drugs — and sweet tastes register less
studies.ns_score_reason: puts laboratory numbers on the much-discussed "food noise" effect, but cross-sectional with fewer than 30 people per group.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Seventy-nine adults with obesity were tested in three groups: eligible for but not yet taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist (n=27), one month into treatment (n=25), and six months in (n=27). They completed laboratory measures of taste thresholds, taste intensity and pleasantness, fat taste, chemesthesis, smell and salivary responses, plus questionnaires on food noise, cue responsivity, craving and food reward. Sweet detection thresholds were higher in both treated groups — they needed more sugar to notice it — while most other chemosensory measures were essentially unchanged. Six-month users reported markedly less food noise, craving, cue responsivity and food reward, and ate less.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests these drugs work mainly on the wanting and the mental chatter around food rather than by making food taste different — with one specific exception for sweetness.
studies.pitch_angle: The lead is the dissociation: on GLP-1 drugs, food does not taste worse, it just stops shouting. Open on the now-familiar patient description of the "quiet" in their head. Call Richard Mattes (Purdue), a long-standing chemosensory researcher, and ask whether the blunted sweet threshold is cause or consequence of eating less sugar.
studies.wider_angle: A features piece for a general-interest or food outlet on the science of "food noise" as a newly legitimized psychological construct — where the questionnaire came from, what it measures, and what it implies for people who have it without ever taking a drug.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional group comparison, not a randomized trial — no one was followed through treatment, so selection effects are plausible; small N per group; dietary intake and food noise self-reported; senior author declares extensive food-industry consulting and funding (Grain Foods Foundation, Almond Board of California, General Mills, Mars Food and others).

studies.title: Boosting a language region of the brain makes metaphors harder to understand
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean causal manipulation with a backwards-seeming result; small, single-session, between-subjects design.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Forty participants received either high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation over the left inferior frontal gyrus (n=20) or sham stimulation (n=20), then rated how comprehensible they found metaphorical sentences ("Passion is a storm"), literal ones ("A gorilla is an ape") and nonsense ones ("Depression is a party"). Anodal stimulation, which raises neuronal excitability, made metaphors seem *less* comprehensible. Literal and nonsensical sentences were unaffected.
studies.why_it_matters: It implicates the brain's semantic control hub causally in figurative language — and shows that turning the volume up on a brain region can degrade, not improve, the behavior it supports.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell the paradox: stimulate the brain's meaning-control center and poetry stops making sense. Open on the metaphor itself — what has to happen in the head for "passion is a storm" to land. Call Hamad Al-Azary (Lawrence Technological University) and ask what selective excitation of semantic control actually does, and why the right hemisphere's traditional starring role in metaphor now looks overstated.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist or long-read outlet: the persistent credibility problem of tDCS. Small samples, sham blinding, effects that flip direction between studies — a piece examining whether brain stimulation findings like this one survive replication, and what the field is doing about it.
studies.caveats: Small N (40 total, 20 per arm); between-subjects rather than within-subjects design; single stimulation session; subjective comprehensibility ratings rather than objective comprehension measures; no active control site.

studies.title: Survivors of the Nova festival attack are being studied from weeks after the trauma to two years on
studies.ns_score_reason: an extraordinary and probably unrepeatable cohort design, including people who were on psychoactive drugs during the trauma; but it is a protocol with no results yet.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)
studies.the_study: The Nova Protocol describes a multimodal longitudinal study of civilian survivors of the 7 October 2023 attack on the Nova music festival, plus a sociocultural comparison group, running from the first weeks after the event to roughly 24 months. Assessments combine repeated clinical questionnaires (PCL-5, K6), wearable-sensor monitoring, ecological momentary assessment, saliva endocrine and inflammatory markers, structural and functional MRI, cardiac interoception paradigms, reinforcement-learning tasks and qualitative interviews. Crucially, many survivors were acutely under the influence of psychoactive substances during and after the attack, creating a naturalistic — not randomized — window on how drug states shape trauma encoding.
studies.why_it_matters: Prospective data starting weeks after a mass trauma with a narrowly defined shared exposure is almost never obtainable; if the cohort holds, it could test which early markers predict who develops PTSD, and whether being on MDMA or LSD during a trauma alters the outcome.
studies.pitch_angle: A cohort that should not exist: hundreds of people exposed to the same catastrophic event within hours of each other, many of them on psychedelics at the time, now wired to sensors and scanners for two years. The hook is the uncomfortable question the researchers themselves flag — does a drug state at the moment of trauma protect or amplify? Call Roee Admon or Roy Salomon (University of Haifa). Frame strictly as a study to watch, with no results yet.
studies.wider_angle: For a magazine or specialist psychotrauma outlet: the ethics of studying survivors while they are still acutely traumatized. Who consents, who declines, how researchers handle the risk of re-traumatization through repeated assessment, and what the PRISMO and 9/11 cohorts learned about long-term participant burden.
studies.caveats: Protocol paper — no findings reported; substance exposure was self-selected and self-reported, so any drug-related association is confounded; survivors are self-selecting volunteers; the comparison group is sociocultural, not exposure-matched; findings will be correlational only, as the authors state.

studies.title: Anxious people don't get the usual relief of bad imagined futures fading
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely interesting asymmetry in how anxiety handles the imagined future, but reported across four linked experiments with unstated sample sizes.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Across four experiments, researchers compared ways of getting people to imagine specific future events, then tracked how the emotion attached to those imagined events decayed over one week or one month. Sentence completion and open association produced more vivid, more plausible, more emotionally charged future events than the standard recombination paradigm. With the more realistic method and a one-week follow-up, people low in anxiety showed the classic "fading affect bias" — negative imagined futures lost their emotional sting faster than positive ones — whereas highly anxious participants showed no such asymmetry.
studies.why_it_matters: The fading affect bias is usually described as a property of memory; extending it to the imagined future, and finding it absent in anxiety, suggests one reason dreaded scenarios stay vivid for some people and dissolve for others.
studies.pitch_angle: Most of us are quietly protected by a bias that lets imagined disasters lose their charge within a week — and anxious people appear to lack it. Open on the 3am rehearsal of a feared conversation. Call Lei Mo's group at South China Normal University and ask whether the effect is about the imagining or the remembering of the imagining.
studies.wider_angle: For a psychology or wellbeing outlet: a piece on episodic future thinking as a therapeutic target — how clinicians are already using imagined futures in treatment for depression and anxiety, and how methodological choices (sentence completion versus recombination) change what participants actually feel.
studies.caveats: Sample sizes not reported in the abstract; anxiety measured by questionnaire grouping rather than clinical diagnosis; emotion ratings entirely self-reported; short follow-up (one week for the key result); the one-month experiment found nothing, which the authors attribute to method rather than absence of effect.

studies.title: Your baseline cortisol decides whether stress wrecks your memory
studies.ns_score_reason: offers a plausible explanation for years of contradictory stress-and-memory results; two modest lab experiments.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Participants learned pairs of unrelated words with negative or neutral meaning and later completed an associative recognition test. In Experiment 1 (n=63) stress was induced before learning; in Experiment 2 (n=56) before recall. Stress before retrieval clearly impaired associative memory. Across both experiments, a larger cortisol surge predicted more false alarms — confidently "recognizing" pairs that never occurred — whereas a higher resting cortisol level predicted fewer. Baseline cortisol moderated the effect: only people with low baseline levels were hurt by a big stress response.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the reason stress-memory studies keep disagreeing is that the same stress response does different things depending on where a person starts, and that stress mainly damages the ability to tell a real memory from a plausible lure.
studies.pitch_angle: Same stress, opposite memory outcome, depending on your resting hormone level — and the damage shows up as confident false memories rather than blanks. Open on an exam or a police interview. Call Jiongjiong Yang (Peking University) and ask whether baseline cortisol could explain the wider replication mess in stress research.
studies.wider_angle: For a legal or criminal-justice-focused outlet: what this means for eyewitness testimony, where stressed witnesses are questioned precisely when their false alarm rate may be highest. A reported piece with memory researchers and interviewing specialists.
studies.caveats: Small N per experiment (63 and 56); single-center laboratory paradigm with word pairs, far from real-world memory; between-groups stress manipulation; salivary cortisol is a noisy single-sample measure; population is likely young university students.

studies.title: Sending clowns into dementia wards changes how families experience visiting
studies.ns_score_reason: a warm, vivid, genuinely unexamined question (the effect on relatives, not patients), but qualitative and small.
studies.media_check: Not widely covered ✓ (0 news hits)
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers interviewed 11 family members and 20 staff across four long-term care homes in eastern Australia about "elder clowning" — trained performers who improvise individualized, person-centered interactions with residents who have dementia. Two themes emerged: the emotional experience of visiting was transformed, easing dread before visits and distress afterwards; and shared moments of laughter supported reminiscence, memory-making and family connection. Relatives also picked up dementia-specific communication techniques from watching the clowns and used them independently.
studies.why_it_matters: Interventions for dementia are evaluated on the person with dementia; this is early evidence that the benefit spills over to the relatives who do most of the emotional work — and that the spillover includes transferable skills.
studies.pitch_angle: The image sells it: a professional clown gets a response from a mother who has not responded to her own daughter in months. Lead on the quoted moment — "someone's acknowledged my mum". Call Sarah Roberts and Michelle DiGiacomo at UTS's IMPACCT group, and ask what exactly the clowns do that relatives can copy.
studies.wider_angle: For an arts-and-health or general-interest outlet: the professionalization of medical clowning, from pediatric wards to dementia care — how performers are trained, what the trial evidence actually shows, and why some families decline to take part at all.
studies.caveats: Small N (11 family members, 20 staff); qualitative interviews with self-selected participants likely to view the program favorably; four homes in one region; no measurement of outcomes in the residents themselves; no control condition.

studies.title: What is actually happening in the brain when blindness brings hallucinations
studies.ns_score_reason: an under-covered condition that readers find arresting, but this is a review rather than new data.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)
studies.the_study: This review synthesizes neuroimaging, neurophysiological, structural and biochemical evidence on Charles Bonnet syndrome, in which people losing their sight experience vivid visual hallucinations without psychiatric illness. The authors conclude the evidence points to cortical hyperexcitability and compensatory reorganization following visual deprivation, with brain-wide changes in connectivity extending beyond visual cortex into attentional networks, and probable involvement of GABAergic and cholinergic signaling. Structural changes specific to the syndrome, as opposed to blindness generally, remain elusive.
studies.why_it_matters: Charles Bonnet syndrome is common in sight loss, badly underrecognized, and frequently misread as psychosis by patients and clinicians alike; it is also a natural experiment in what a visual cortex does when starved of input.
studies.pitch_angle: People going blind who see faces, patterns and figures in impossible detail — and who often keep silent for fear of being thought mad. The hook is the mechanism: a visual system so starved of input that it generates its own. Open on a patient who took years to tell an ophthalmologist. Call Geraint Plant (UCL) or D. Samuel Schwarzkopf (Auckland), and ask about the proposal to model the syndrome with deep neural networks deprived of input.
studies.wider_angle: For a general-interest or long-read outlet: hallucination as a normal property of predictive brains. A feature threading Charles Bonnet syndrome together with musical hallucinations in deafness, phantom limbs, and sensory-deprivation experiments — what they collectively say about how much of ordinary perception is invented.
studies.caveats: Narrative review, not primary research; the underlying literature is methodologically heterogeneous and dominated by small samples and case studies; mechanistic claims are inferential.

studies.title: Exercise gives a small but real lift to memory in people with depression
studies.ns_score_reason: first meta-analysis pooling RCTs on this specific outcome, with moderate-certainty evidence; the effect is small and no exercise variable moderated it.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: A three-level meta-analysis of 13 randomized controlled trials (1098 participants) tested whether exercise interventions improve episodic memory — remembering specific events — in people with depression. The pooled effect was small to moderate and statistically robust (Hedges' g = 0.21), with similar gains for immediate and delayed recall. No exercise characteristic — type, intensity, duration, frequency — moderated the effect, and certainty of evidence was rated moderate.
studies.why_it_matters: Memory complaints are one of the most disabling residual features of depression and are poorly addressed by antidepressants; this suggests exercise helps modestly, and that the specific prescription may matter less than doing something.
studies.pitch_angle: The useful nuance is the absence of a dose-response: across 13 trials, nothing about *how* people exercised predicted how much their memory improved. Open on someone in recovery from depression who can function at work but cannot remember last week. Call Xue Xia (University of Health and Rehabilitation Sciences, Qingdao) and ask what "no moderators" really means when the trials are this heterogeneous.
studies.wider_angle: For a health or clinical outlet: cognitive symptoms as the neglected half of depression. Why trials measure mood and not memory, why regulators do not require cognitive endpoints, and what patients say about which symptom bothers them most.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of existing trials; only 13 studies with inconsistent memory instruments; small effect size; short follow-up in component trials; risk of unblinded outcome assessment in exercise RCTs; publication bias hard to exclude at this number of studies.

studies.title: Aggression, insomnia and loneliness explain much of the link between childhood trauma and suicide risk
studies.ns_score_reason: large clinical cohort and a careful mediation model, but cross-sectional, which undercuts the whole idea of mediation.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using 1572 people with a 12-month depressive or anxiety disorder from the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety, researchers tested which psychosocial, personality, lifestyle and biological variables statistically account for the link between childhood trauma severity and either suicidal ideation alone or ideation with an attempt. Childhood trauma raised the odds of ideation (OR 1.51) and, far more, of ideation with an attempt (OR 2.68). Multiple-mediator models cut the direct association by 66 percent and 39 percent respectively, with aggression, insomnia and low social support surviving for both outcomes; interleukin-6 accounted for only a small slice of the attempt pathway.
studies.why_it_matters: It picks out a handful of potentially modifiable links in a chain that is otherwise fixed in the past — though the cross-sectional design means these are statistical, not demonstrated, pathways.
studies.pitch_angle: Childhood trauma nearly triples the odds of a suicide attempt in people with depression or anxiety — and two-thirds of that statistical link runs through things that can, in principle, be treated now: sleep, aggression, isolation. Call Jasper Wiebenga or Brenda Penninx (Amsterdam UMC / NESARC-scale NESDA cohort). Be scrupulous: no clinical claims from cross-sectional mediation.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist psychiatry or policy outlet: the inflammation hypothesis of suicide gets a lukewarm result here, with IL-6 explaining very little. A piece on how immune markers have fared as predictors of suicidal behavior once psychosocial variables are in the model.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional design — the authors themselves note causal inference is not possible, and mediation models require temporal ordering they do not have; childhood trauma is retrospectively recalled; suicide attempts self-reported; clinical sample of people with depressive or anxiety disorders, so it does not generalize to the general population.

studies.title: Cannabis use disorder tracks with suicide attempts — except in people with bipolar disorder, where it barely moves quality of life
studies.ns_score_reason: a nationally representative sample and a genuinely odd dissociation, but secondary analysis of cross-sectional survey data.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI lookup failed
studies.the_study: Drawing on NESARC-III, researchers compared 753 adults with lifetime bipolar I disorder against 35,556 without, across levels of DSM-5 cannabis use disorder severity. Lifetime suicide attempts were reported by 34 percent of people with both bipolar I and severe cannabis use disorder, against 17 percent with severe CUD and no bipolar diagnosis. But while mental health quality of life fell steadily with CUD severity in people without bipolar disorder, in people with bipolar disorder it did not vary with CUD severity at all. Physical health quality of life differed by neither.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests bipolar disorder sets a floor on self-reported mental wellbeing that heavy cannabis use does not lower further, even as the association with lifetime suicide attempts is much stronger — a reminder that quality-of-life scores and risk of harm can come apart.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the dissociation: in bipolar disorder, escalating cannabis problems go with double the rate of suicide attempts but no measurable drop in reported quality of life. Open on why that makes cannabis problems easy for a clinician to miss. Call Ty Schepis (Texas State University) and ask whether it is a ceiling effect in the instrument or something real.
studies.wider_angle: For a drug-policy or health outlet: as cannabis legalizes and potency climbs, what happens to the subgroup for whom it is riskiest? A reported piece on how legalization frameworks handle — or ignore — people with serious mental illness.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of cross-sectional national survey data (cannot establish causation or direction); lifetime diagnoses and lifetime suicide attempts both retrospectively self-reported; NESARC-III data now over a decade old and predates high-potency product markets; bipolar subgroup with severe CUD is small, giving wide confidence intervals.

studies.the_study: Researchers reviewed all 1206 adolescent presentations to a public child and adolescent psychiatric emergency service in Brazil over one year, of which 160 (13 percent) involved adolescents in custodial or semi-custodial detention. Compared with community-living peers, detained adolescents were more likely to present with insomnia (43 versus 19 percent) and suicide attempts (26 versus 18 percent), and carried more stress-related and adjustment disorder, conduct disorder and substance use diagnoses. Agitation, aggression, irritability and disobedience were comparatively *less* frequent, and depression diagnoses were less common (26 versus 35 percent).
studies.why_it_matters: Detained young people are widely assumed to reach mental health services because of disruptive behavior; here they arrive in acute distress, which implies a different kind of screening inside detention facilities.
studies.pitch_angle: The stereotype is aggression; the data say sleeplessness and self-harm. Open on the emergency clinician who expected one and found the other. Call Débora Marques de Miranda (Federal University of Minas Gerais) and ask what a 43 percent insomnia rate inside detention actually reflects — the environment, withdrawal, or trauma.
studies.wider_angle: For a social-affairs or investigative outlet: sleep as a neglected instrument of harm in youth custody. A reported piece on lights, noise, cell checks and night-time distress across juvenile detention systems, and the small but growing literature linking custodial sleep conditions to self-harm.
studies.caveats: Retrospective review of clinical records, single center, one city in Brazil; diagnoses made in emergency conditions; 160 detained adolescents is a modest subgroup; no data on adolescents in detention who never reached the service; findings may not generalize to other justice systems.

studies.ns_score_reason: a mostly null result in a large clinical sample, which is useful and rarely published; limited by uncertainty about whether the tool could detect differences anyway.

studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed C-PEP-3 developmental profiles from 1050 children with autism (834 boys, 216 girls; aged 2–10) assessed in Beijing between 2021 and 2024. After controlling for age and correcting for multiple comparisons, only one of seven developmental domains differed by sex, and only in the youngest group: girls aged 2–3 had smaller delays in cognitive performance than boys (Cohen's d = −0.36). Nothing differed at ages 4–6 or 7–10.
studies.why_it_matters: Sex differences in autism are widely assumed to be pervasive and are increasingly used to explain late diagnosis in girls; in a large Chinese clinical sample they are almost entirely absent on this standard developmental profile — although the authors concede the instrument may be too coarse to detect them.
studies.pitch_angle: A large sample, a careful analysis, and essentially nothing: the story is the null. Open on a clinician looking for the "female autism profile" and not finding it. Call Meixiang Jia (Peking University Sixth Hospital) and ask the honest question — is this about girls, or about the test?
studies.wider_angle: For a general-interest or health outlet: the "female autism phenotype" as a research hypothesis under strain. A feature on how the idea took hold, what it has done for diagnosis rates in girls and women, and how much of it rests on Western, self-selected adult samples.
studies.caveats: Clinical convenience sample from a single association in Beijing; girls under-represented (215 in the analytic sample), reducing power to detect small differences; the instrument's sensitivity to sex-specific patterns is explicitly unverified; cross-sectional and not diagnostic of trajectory; may not generalize beyond Chinese clinical services.

studies.title: People with psychosis are least likely to get the medication that treats opioid addiction
studies.ns_score_reason: a clear, actionable disparity across 12,000 treatment episodes; administrative data with limited clinical detail.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run

studies.the_study: Using US Treatment Episode Dataset-Discharges records from 2016–2022, researchers examined 12,219 adult outpatient substance use treatment discharges involving both opioid use disorder and a comorbid mental disorder. In multilevel models adjusted for opioid-related, treatment, sociodemographic and state-level factors, discharges involving depressive disorders (AOR 1.48) or anxiety disorders (AOR 1.43) were substantially more likely to include planned medication for opioid use disorder than those involving psychotic disorders.
studies.why_it_matters: Medications such as buprenorphine and methadone are the most effective treatment for opioid use disorder, and people with psychosis — already at high risk of early death — appear to be systematically less likely to be offered them.
studies.pitch_angle: Same addiction, same clinics, different treatment depending on which psychiatric label is attached. Open on the clinical assumption doing the work here — that someone with schizophrenia cannot adhere to a medication regimen. Call Jonathan Moore (Florida State University) and ask whether the gap is prescriber judgment, program eligibility rules, or something else in the data.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-policy or investigative outlet: the diagnostic hierarchy inside addiction services. A reported piece on how people with severe mental illness fall between mental health and substance use systems, and whether integrated dual-diagnosis programs close the gap.
studies.caveats: Administrative discharge data with no information on why medication was or was not planned; "planned MOUD" is not the same as receiving it; cross-sectional and observational; states report to TEDS-D inconsistently; US-specific system findings.

studies.the_study: Researchers assessed 455 Dutch veterans seeking treatment at four national psychotrauma centers, validating a Dutch version of the Expressions of Moral Injury Scale – Military Version and running a latent profile analysis. The scale supported two factors — moral injury directed at the self and at others. Three profiles emerged: subclinical (21 percent), moderate (48 percent) and high (31 percent) moral injury and PTSD together. Higher profiles carried more comorbid psychopathology and significantly poorer family functioning.
studies.why_it_matters: Moral injury — the damage done by doing, witnessing or failing to prevent something that violates one's own moral code — is increasingly treated as distinct from fear-based PTSD; this shows it travels with PTSD in nearly four in five treatment-seeking veterans and shows up in how families function.
studies.pitch_angle: Not fear but guilt and betrayal: a look at the 31 percent of treatment-seeking veterans carrying both severe PTSD and severe moral injury, and at the family members who register it. Call Marissa de Goede or Paul Boelen (Utrecht University / ARQ Centrum'45) and ask why PTSD treatments that target fear extinction often fail this group.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist or current-affairs outlet: moral injury beyond the military. Health workers after the pandemic, refugee-camp staff, aid workers and police — a feature on a construct migrating out of veteran care and into civilian professions, and whether it will hold up there.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, treatment-seeking sample (not representative of all veterans); confirmatory factor analysis fit indices only adequate; family functioning and all symptoms self-reported at pre-intake; no causal direction between moral injury and family strain; Dutch service population may not generalize.

studies.the_study: This review synthesizes evidence on emotional intelligence in negotiation and argues the literature shows an "EI paradox": emotional intelligence is fairly consistently associated with relational outcomes such as trust, rapport and satisfaction, but not with economic outcomes such as profit or value claimed. The proposed explanation is that the same capacities that help coordinate and create value also increase accommodation, regulation costs and susceptibility to being emotionally played. trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**

- **Insomnia keeps turning up as a marker rather than a mechanism.** The previous digest's harmonized Australian–Swedish cohorts found that broken sleep, not oxygen desaturation, carried the depression signal (PMID 42663413). The new batch pushes that further in two directions: the 10-year PRISMO military cohort finds insomnia rises and falls *with* PTSD and depression but never precedes them (PMID 42750113), and insomnia appears as one of three surviving statistical mediators between childhood trauma and suicide attempt (PMID 42637149), plus the dominant presenting complaint among detained adolescents in a Brazilian psychiatric emergency service (PMID 42748415). Across two runs, insomnia is everywhere and causal in nothing.
- **Nulls that puncture policy assumptions.** The MH17 "closure" null (PMID 42635331) and the precision psychiatry readiness audit (PMID 42657684) in the previous run are matched by the new digest's finding that state parity laws and larger mental health budgets shift only cost-related barriers, not treatment receipt, unmet need, overdose or suicide mortality (PMID 42750086), and by the near-total absence of sex differences in developmental profiles of 1050 autistic children (PMID 42748595). Both batches are dominated by well-powered results that decline to confirm the expected story.
- **Exercise as a modest, non-specific lever.** The previous run's dissociation between mental and physical fatigue in predicting activity (PMID 42543096) sits next to two new items: 12 minutes of weekly vigorous activity matching 150 minutes of moderate activity for mortality in 147,414 accelerometer-tracked adults (PMID 42745313), and a small but robust memory benefit of exercise in depression with no moderation by type, intensity, duration or frequency (PMID 42641961). The recurring message is that intensity and specifics matter less than the units guidelines are written in imply.

**Advances**

- **Trauma cohort science gets more ambitious.** The previous digest's post-trauma intervention work was analogue-lab (psychological first aid, PMID 42561812) or retrospective-longitudinal (MH17, PMID 42635331). The new Nova Protocol (PMID 42735067) is prospective from weeks after a mass-casualty event, with wearables, MRI, endocrine markers and a naturalistic drug-state exposure — the design that PFA-style questions actually need. The PRISMO cohort (PMID 42750113) supplies the decade-long comparator.
- **PTSD's framing shifts from fear to morality.** Following the previous run's grief-structure work (PMIDs 42635331, 42635333), the new validation and latent profile analysis of moral injury in 455 Dutch veterans (PMID 42734648) extends the same move — decomposing a broad distress category into distinguishable constructs with their own correlates, here poorer family functioning.
- **From correlational brain markers to causal manipulation.** Where the previous batch offered observational signatures (post-stroke EEG, PMID 42663449; DTI-ALPS and antipsychotic polypharmacy, PMID 42551238), the new digest includes a direct causal intervention: anodal stimulation of the left inferior frontal gyrus making metaphors *less* comprehensible (PMID 42667874) — with the same replication-fragility caveat attached.

**Counterpoints**

- **Interventions that work, but not on what was measured.** The previous run's storyline was psychological help failing or backfiring (PMIDs 42546730, 42561812). The new batch complicates it: elder clowning transformed the experience of *relatives* rather than being evaluated on residents (PMID 42749305), and the Arabic PTSD Coach app reduced sadness while leaving happiness untouched (PMID 42747789). Benefit is real but lands off the target the trial was pointed at.
- **Sleep as a treatment target.** The previous digest implied insomnia was the causally relevant sleep variable for mood (PMID 42663413); the new within-person modeling of PRISMO (PMID 42750113) argues it is a co-traveler that does not predict later PTSD or depression at all. These two need reconciling, and the tension is itself a story.

**New themes**

- **Heritability and genetics return.** The Danish twin estimate of 0.60 for postpartum depression (PMID 42648551) opens a genetic strand entirely absent from the previous digest.
- **Service-level inequity.** People with psychotic disorders are markedly less likely to have planned medication for opioid use disorder than those with depression or anxiety (PMID 42743214), joining the parity-law null (PMID 42750086) to make access and delivery, rather than mechanism, a live theme.
- **Appetite, taste and GLP-1 drugs.** Laboratory measures putting numbers on "food noise" and finding blunted sweet detection but otherwise intact chemosensation (PMID 42641845) is new territory for this digest.
- **Hallucination and deprived cortex.** The Charles Bonnet syndrome review (PMID 42747922) restores a perception-science strand that in the previous run was represented by featureless object tracking (PMID 42537447).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Study after study in this batch finds that a treatment or policy moves one dial and leaves the obvious neighboring dial untouched — and that which dial you chose to measure decides whether anything "worked." GLP-1 drugs quiet food noise, craving and reward while food itself tastes much the same (PMID 42641845); an Arabic self-help app lowered sadness with no model fitting happiness at all (PMID 42747789); in bipolar I disorder, escalating cannabis use disorder goes with double the rate of lifetime suicide attempts yet no change in self-rated mental health quality of life (PMID 42664567); elder clowning's documented benefit falls on visiting relatives, who were never the intended outcome (PMID 42749305); exercise in depression lifts episodic memory with no dose-response (PMID 42641961); and mental health parity laws remove the price barrier while treatment receipt and unmet need stay flat (PMID 42750086).

**Why pitch this now:** Regulators, insurers and app developers are all currently deciding which endpoints count as evidence of benefit in mental health, and this batch shows the standard composite measures — quality-of-life scores, mood scales, "treatment receipt" — systematically missing effects that patients and families describe clearly.

**Angle:** A reported feature on outcome measurement as the hidden decision in mental health research: who picks the endpoint, why negative and positive affect were ever assumed to be one scale, and what gets classified as ineffective simply because nobody measured the thing that changed. Aimed at readers who have filled in a PHQ-9 or been told a treatment "didn't show a benefit."

**Potential headlines:**
- The treatments are working, just not on the things being measured
- An app made people less sad and no happier, and that broke the scoring sheet
- Your treatment may be helping in a way the questionnaire cannot see

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the Mind section can carry the GLP-1 food-noise and sadness-versus-happiness findings as concrete anchors for a measurement story readers will recognize from their own forms.
- **STAT** — endpoint selection is squarely its beat, and the parity-law null plus the opioid-medication disparity give it a regulatory and payer spine.
- **Scientific American** — well suited to the conceptual core, that negative and positive affect and quality of life and harm run on partly separate systems.
- **Knowable Magazine** — built for exactly this kind of "how the field decided what to count" explainer, with room for the history of the instruments themselves.

# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-17 | **Studies reviewed:** 22
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-09-17

---

### Study 1: Postpartum depression is strongly heritable, Danish twin study finds
**PMID:** 42648551 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

All core numbers check out: 10,418 female twins (5209 pairs), born January 1949–December 2000, MZ probandwise concordance 0.22 vs DZ 0.11, heritability 0.60 (95% CI 0.46–0.75), unique environment 0.40, and the "15 concordant pairs" figure (10 MZ + 5 DZ).

**Issue A. Comparison to major depression** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a genetic contribution on a par with that of major depression"
- **Abstract says:** Nothing about the heritability of major depression; it reports only that heritability of PPD was 0.60 and that "its underlying causes and degree of heritability remain unclear."
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only, and the direction is questionable — published twin heritability for major depression is usually put around 0.35–0.40, i.e. lower than 0.60, so "on a par" may understate the contrast the study actually implies.
- **Suggested fix:** "a substantial genetic contribution — around 60 per cent of the variation in liability — reframes it as a condition women are predisposed to"

**Issue B. Incomplete competing-interest disclosure** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "author funding from the Novo Nordisk and Lundbeck Foundations, with Lundbeck lecture fees declared"
- **Abstract says:** "Carolyn E Cesta reports a relationship with Merck AB that includes: speaking and lecture fees."
- **Problem:** The digest captures the main funders and the Lundbeck relationship but omits a second industry relationship (Merck AB) declared in the same statement.
- **Suggested fix:** "...with Lundbeck lecture fees declared by the senior author and Merck AB lecture fees by a co-author."

---

### Study 2: Insomnia travels with PTSD and depression but does not seem to cause them
**PMID:** 42750113 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 846, the six timepoints, the RI-CLPM design, the null insomnia→PTSD/depression cross-lagged paths, the significant within-time within-person covariances at all timepoints, and the small reciprocal PTSD–depression effects all match. The hedged headline ("does not seem to cause them") is consistent with the authors' own wording ("co-fluctuates with, but does not causally drive"). Framing is consistent with the abstract.

---

### Study 3: Twelve minutes of vigorous exercise a week matches 150 minutes of moderate activity
**PMID:** 42745313 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 147,414, ages 40–74, NAKO + UK Biobank, mean follow-up 7.9 years, 5,545 deaths, HR 0.70 for 150 min/week moderate, ~510 min light / 12 min vigorous equivalence, and the 18–30% reallocation figures are all correct. The Bayer/Siemens Healthineers disclosure is correctly carried into Caveats.

**Issue A. Headline omits the outcome and implies equivalence of effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Twelve minutes of vigorous exercise a week matches 150 minutes of moderate activity"
- **Abstract says:** "Compared with no activity, 150 min per week of moderate-intensity activity was associated with lower mortality (HR: 0.70…). Similar associations were observed for approximately 510 min per week of light-intensity activity or 12 min per week of vigorous-intensity activity."
- **Problem:** The equivalence is specifically for the *association with all-cause mortality* in an observational pooled cohort. Unqualified, "matches" reads as a general health-benefit equivalence and as a demonstrated effect.
- **Suggested fix:** "Twelve minutes of vigorous activity a week is linked to the same lower death risk as 150 minutes of moderate activity"

**Issue B. Device and wear-period details not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "pooled wrist accelerometer data" / "baseline activity measured once, over about a week"
- **Abstract says:** "individually pooled baseline device-measured physical activity"; "the largest pooled accelerometer dataset to date." No placement or wear-duration specified.
- **Problem:** Wrist placement and the ~7-day wear window are plausible for both cohorts but are unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "pooled device-measured (accelerometer) activity data" and, in Caveats, "baseline activity measured once, over a short wear period."

**Issue C. NS fit score and section fit** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10"
- **Problem:** The evidence quality supports a high score (very large, device-measured, prospective), so 7 is defensible on rigour. The mismatch is placement: this is an all-cause mortality paper with no mind or brain outcome, filed under New Scientist Mind. Either the section assignment or the score rationale needs a line acknowledging that.
- **Suggested fix:** Keep 7/10 but flag for a Health rather than Mind slot, or note "no cognitive or mental-health outcome measured."

---

### Study 4: "Food noise" is quieter in people six months into GLP-1 drugs — and sweet tastes register less
**PMID:** 42641845 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Group sizes (27/25/27, total 79), the sweet-threshold result in both treated groups, and the lower cue responsivity, craving, food reward and energy intake in 6-month users are accurately reported.

**Issue A. Causal mechanism language from a cross-sectional design** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It suggests these drugs work mainly on the wanting and the mental chatter around food rather than by making food taste different"
- **Abstract says:** "In this cross-sectional study… Overall, GLP-1RA use was associated with lower food salience, cravings, cue responsiveness, food reward, and energy intake, while chemosensory differences were limited mainly to sweet taste detection."
- **Problem:** Three separate groups compared at one timepoint cannot establish how the drugs work; the authors keep to "associated with." The Caveats flag the design, but the body text asserts a mechanism anyway.
- **Suggested fix:** "It hints that the difference between treated and untreated people lies in wanting and the mental chatter around food rather than in how food tastes — with one exception for sweetness — though a cross-sectional comparison cannot show what the drugs are doing."

**Issue B. "Markedly" overstates the food-noise result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Six-month users reported markedly less food noise, craving, cue responsivity and food reward, and ate less."
- **Abstract says:** "Food Noise Questionnaire scores were lower in 6-month users than in pre-use controls (P = .026)."
- **Problem:** p = .026 on a questionnaire score in a ~27-per-group comparison does not support "markedly"; no effect size is given.
- **Suggested fix:** "Six-month users reported significantly lower food noise, along with lower craving, cue responsivity, food reward and energy intake."

**Issue C. Fat-taste exception dropped** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "while most other chemosensory measures were essentially unchanged"
- **Abstract says:** "Suprathreshold taste intensity, taste hedonics, olfactory function, and chemesthesis were largely unchanged, except for a limited fat-intensity difference at medium linoleic acid concentration."
- **Problem:** There was a second, smaller chemosensory difference; the digest's "one specific exception for sweetness" framing in Why it matters therefore isn't quite right.
- **Suggested fix:** "…while other chemosensory measures were largely unchanged, apart from a limited fat-intensity difference at one linoleic acid concentration."

**Issue D. NS fit score too high for the design** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — puts laboratory numbers on the much-discussed 'food noise' effect, but cross-sectional with fewer than 30 people per group."
- **Problem:** The headline finding (less food noise) rests on a self-report questionnaire in a cross-sectional comparison of ~27 people per group, with no one followed through treatment. That is exactly the profile the 7+ threshold is meant to catch.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 5/10, with the rationale "first laboratory chemosensory numbers on food noise, but cross-sectional, tiny groups, self-reported primary outcome."

---

### Study 5: Boosting a language region of the brain makes metaphors harder to understand
**PMID:** 42667874 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 40 (20 anodal, 20 sham), HD-tDCS over LIFG, the three sentence types with the exact example items, and the selective reduction in metaphor comprehensibility are all accurate. "Causal role" is the authors' own language, so the Why it matters framing is fair.

**Issue A. Right-hemisphere claim not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "why the right hemisphere's traditional starring role in metaphor now looks overstated"
- **Abstract says:** "the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG), which is traditionally considered a literal language semantic control region"
- **Problem:** The abstract frames the novelty as LIFG involvement in metaphor, not as a rebuttal of right-hemisphere accounts. Unverifiable from abstract only, and the study included no right-hemisphere condition or control site.
- **Suggested fix:** "ask what selective excitation of a region traditionally tied to literal semantic control tells us about how figurative meaning is retrieved."

---

### Study 6: Survivors of the Nova festival attack are being studied from weeks after the trauma to two years on
**PMID:** 42735067 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Correctly identified as a protocol paper with no results; the assessment battery, PCL-5/K6 primary outcomes, ~24-month span, sociocultural comparison group, and the authors' own statement that findings will be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects are all accurately conveyed.

**Issue A. Named drugs and "psychedelics" go beyond the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "whether being on MDMA or LSD during a trauma alters the outcome" / "many of them on psychedelics at the time"
- **Abstract says:** "Many survivors also reported being under the acute influence of psychoactive substances during the attack and the following hours."
- **Problem:** No specific substances are named. Unverifiable from abstract only, and naming MDMA and LSD sharpens the hook beyond the stated exposure.
- **Suggested fix:** "whether being under the acute influence of psychoactive substances during a trauma alters the outcome" / "many of them under the influence of psychoactive drugs at the time."

**Issue B. Cohort size and assessment terminology** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "hundreds of people exposed to the same catastrophic event within hours of each other" / "ecological momentary assessment"
- **Abstract says:** No survivor sample size is given (the 370+ figure refers to attendees killed); the method is listed as "ecological assessments."
- **Problem:** The cohort size is unverifiable, and "ecological momentary assessment" is a specific method the abstract does not name.
- **Suggested fix:** "a cohort of survivors of one catastrophic event, all exposed within a narrow time window" and "ecological assessments."

---

### Study 7: Anxious people don't get the usual relief of bad imagined futures fading
**PMID:** 42750110 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The four-experiment structure, the one-week/one-month follow-ups, and the key interaction (greater emotional fading for negative future events in the low-anxiety group, absent in the high-anxiety group) are accurate. Caveats correctly note that sample sizes are absent from the abstract.

**Issue A. "More vivid" is not among the reported differences** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Sentence completion and open association produced more vivid, more plausible, more emotionally charged future events than the standard recombination paradigm."
- **Abstract says:** "the sentence completion method elicited future events perceived as more likely to occur and with greater perceived impact, inducing stronger emotions"; open association "evoked stronger emotions and had a larger perceived impact on participants, with a greater probability of occurrence."
- **Problem:** Vividness was not a reported outcome; also, only sentence completion is explicitly compared with recombination in Experiment 1a.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sentence completion produced future events rated as more likely, more impactful and more emotionally charged than the standard recombination paradigm, and open association did the same."

**Issue B. Attribution of the null one-month result to method** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the one-month experiment found nothing, which the authors attribute to method rather than absence of effect"
- **Abstract says:** "Experiment 1b used a sentence completion task with a one-month follow-up, but found no significant emotional fading difference between positive and negative future events."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports the null but does not state an explanation; the method interpretation is inferred from the sequence of experiments. Also, 1b differs from 2b in both method *and* follow-up length.
- **Suggested fix:** "the one-month experiment (a different method and a longer interval) found no such difference."

---

### Study 8: Your baseline cortisol decides whether stress wrecks your memory
**PMID:** 42749210 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 63 (pre-encoding) and 56 (pre-retrieval), the significant pre-retrieval impairment, cortisol reactivity positively predicting false alarms, baseline cortisol negatively predicting them, and the lure-discrimination interpretation are all accurate.

**Issue A. Headline asserts causation for a measured moderator** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Your baseline cortisol decides whether stress wrecks your memory"
- **Abstract says:** "baseline cortisol levels moderated the effect of stress on memory performance. When the baseline cortisol levels were lower, a greater cortisol reactivity was associated with a higher FA rate."
- **Problem:** Stress was manipulated, but baseline cortisol is an observed individual difference; "decides" is causal language for a correlational moderator. "Wrecks your memory" also overstates a shift in false-alarm rates on a word-pair associative recognition task.
- **Suggested fix:** "Your baseline cortisol may shape whether a stress response distorts your memory"

**Issue B. "Only" overstates the moderation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Baseline cortisol moderated the effect: only people with low baseline levels were hurt by a big stress response."
- **Abstract says:** "When the baseline cortisol levels were lower, a greater cortisol reactivity was associated with a higher FA rate in both experiments."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports the association at lower baseline; it does not state that there was no association at higher baseline.
- **Suggested fix:** "Baseline cortisol moderated the effect: a big stress response was linked to more false alarms mainly in people with lower baseline levels."

**Issue C. Caveat inconsistent with the measures used** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "salivary cortisol is a noisy single-sample measure"
- **Abstract says:** Reports both "baseline cortisol levels" and "cortisol reactivity," which requires at least two samples.
- **Problem:** The caveat contradicts the design implied by the abstract; the sampling schedule is otherwise unverifiable.
- **Suggested fix:** "salivary cortisol is a noisy marker and the exact sampling schedule is not given in the abstract."

### Study 9: Sending clowns into dementia wards changes how families experience visiting

### Study 12: Aggression, insomnia and loneliness explain much of the link between childhood trauma and suicide risk

**Issue C. Single-author paper described in plural** — Severity: Minor

- **Abstract says:** Single author (Smolinski R), HHL Leipzig; the paper uses "We argue" and "We propose" despite sole authorship.
- **Problem:** Not an error, but the digest should make clear to a commissioning editor that this is a single-author opinion piece in an *Current Opinion* series, which bears on the NS fit score.
- **Suggested fix:** Add to Caveats: "single-author opinion review in a Current Opinion series, not a systematic synthesis."

### Cross-cutting notes for the section editor

1. **Headline-versus-body drift is the dominant failure mode.** In studies 8, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18 and 20 the body text is accurate and appropriately hedged while the headline or pitch line asserts something stronger. Studies 12, 13 and 20 are the three where the headline could leave a reader with the wrong finding, and those need rewriting before pitching, not just softening.

2. **Two entries have score problems.** Study 4 at 7/10 rests on a cross-sectional comparison of ~27 people per group with a self-reported primary outcome; recommended 5/10. Study 3 at 7/10 is defensible on evidence quality but has no mind or brain outcome and looks misfiled under New Scientist Mind.

3. **Twelve claims are unverifiable from the abstract alone** and should be marked as such in the digest rather than stated flat: the major-depression heritability comparison (1), accelerometer placement and wear period (3), the right-hemisphere framing (5), named substances and cohort size (6), the one-month null explanation (7), moderator list and priority claim (11), the OR scaling (12), the self-isolation scoring (18), and the toilet-privacy mechanism (21). Study 12's OR scaling is the one that most needs resolving with the authors, because the pitch's central multiplier depends on it.

4. **Disclosure handling was good overall** — studies 3 and 4 both carried industry funding into Caveats. Study 1 missed one of two declared industry relationships.
